speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the statement made by the Prime Minister on October 7, 1966, I am now tabling copies of the formal agreement between myself as Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources representing the government of Canada, and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Ltd., embodying specific undertakings made by the company relating to its application for a certificate of public convenience and necessity and licences for the exportation and importation of gas in connection with the great lakes project.
I am also tabling a letter dated September 22,	1966, addressed to me by Trans-
Canada Pipe Lines, containing the company's representations and the undertakings upon which the agreement is based.
Hon. members will recall that in August the National Energy Board reported to the governor in council upon Trans-Canada's application, indicating that it was prepared to issue a certificate and licences, and drawing attention to certain issues of public policy extending beyond its field of responsibility. On August 25 the Prime Minister stated that the government had not approved the issuance of these authorizations by the board, for
the basic reason that once the proposed pipe line system through the United States had been built it would almost inevitably become the main line, and that this would not be in accord with either the spirit of the policy laid down by parliament in the act incorporating Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Ltd. or in the national interest.
Following this announcement Trans-Canada made the representations and the undertakings set forth in the letter of September 22 which I have tabled. The undertakings were as follows:
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
(1)	Trans-Canada guarantees that more than 50 per cent of the volume of gas required to supply eastern Canada will be transported through its main line traversing northern Ontario;
(2)	Trans-Canada also agrees to accept as a target that by the end of 1976 that figure would be raised to 60 per cent, and further agrees that its long range objective should be to transport 65 per cent of the volumes for eastern Canada through the northern Ontario facilities;
(3)	To carry out this undertaking, Trans-Canada would commence looping the northern Ontario line by 1970 and would complete this looping in stages thereafter in accordance with the development of the Canadian market;
(4)	Trans-Canada offered to deposit the shares representing its 50 per cent ownership in the Great Lakes Gas Transmission Company with a trustee under terms and conditions acceptable to the government, to ensure that the company could never dispose of its interest in great lakes without the prior approval of the government of Canada.
In addition, Trans-Canada informed the government that American Natural Gas Company, its partner in the Great Lakes Gas Transmission Company, guaranteed the purchase from this jointly owned company of an additional 100 million cubic feet of Canadian gas per day for a period of 25 years, commencing with 50 million cubic feet per day in 1969 and increasing to 100 million cubic feet per day in 1970. The company also referred to other good prospects it had for selling gas in the export markets.

October 28, 1966
Natural Gas
The National Energy Board was asked to comment upon these undertakings and representations, having regard to the reasons for the government's decision as expressed on August 25. The board, in its reply, was of the opinion that the undertakings by Trans-Canada would remove the possibility that the great lakes line might become in effect the main line of Trans-Canada and should put at rest the question whether Trans-Canada's participation in the great lakes project is consistent with the special act of parliament by which Trans-Canada was incorporated.
In summary, the board stated that in its view-
-the undertakings given and representations tnade by Trans-Canada are an adequate and acceptable response to the reasons given in the government statement of August 25 for not approving the certificate and licences sought by the company.
On October 4 the Prime Minister announced that having regard to the advice of the board already referred to, the government had approved the issuance of a certificate of public convenience and necessity and export and import licences to Trans-Canada as recommended by the board, subject to the undertakings being incorporated in an agreement between Trans-Canada and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources acceptable to the minister.
The agreement I have tabled incorporates the aforesaid undertakings in such a form as to bind Trans-Canada to always maintain in Canada the main line for the supply of western Canadian gas to eastern Canada. These undertakings will be under the continuous surveillance of the National Energy Board and would be taken into consideration at the time of any future applications of Trans-Canada. There is also a clause stating that Trans-Canada will be liable to the amount of at least $1 million for each breach of the agreement. This does not imply, of course, any lack of faith in the desire or capacity of Trans-Canada to honour the agreement.
I would like to make it clear that this decision was taken solely on the undertakings given by Trans-Canada and not on the representations as to future exports, however attractive they may be. The house is also well aware that the National Energy Board Act provides that only gas which has been declared by the board surplus to the reasonably foreseeable requirements of Canada can be exported. No applications have been received covering these additional exports, and while the government has every confidence in the

future potential of our gas reserves, until such time as proper applications are filed and processed there cannot be any implied commitment in respect of future exports.
I believe that the great lakes project as now contemplated will provide growth markets for western Canadian gas and assist industrial development in eastern Canada. It will provide additional security for eastern Canadian consumers by having two lines by which western Canadian gas could be transmitted to them, and will also provide delivery by the shorter great lakes route to industrial markets and storage fields in southwestern Ontario.
May I express the hope that hon. members and the public will agree with us that the government was motivated in its decision by its desire to keep the line through northern Ontario as the main link between western Canadian reserves and eastern Canada, while providing for the maximum utilization of Canadian gas in Canada and in the export market, and the incentive for continuous development of our gas reserves.

Mr. Speaker, one of the great reserves in Canada's natural resource wealth is western gas. These reserves are increasing each year. With the discoveries now being made in northern Alberta and the explorations being carried on in the Northwest Territories and British Columbia it is obvious that our surplus gas reserves go far beyond any needs of Canada for the foreseeable future. These resources must be made available to Canadians first, but the verified surpluses must likewise be made available to the export markets.
If we do not do this we will be cutting off our nose to save our face. It is not a question of Americanism one way or the other; it is a question of sound economics. You do not store something in the bowels of the earth which you will not have any use for, if you can make economic use of it elsewhere. We are agreed that there must be built-in guarantees to fill the needs of eastern Canada and northern Ontario. In this particular case, however, I must commend the minister for the decisions he has taken in rejecting the first proposal of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and turning it back for a new proposal containing certain basic requirements which he considered essential.
It is known to us that the National Energy Board approved the first proposals. The government in overruling those first proposals in this instance has shown what to me seems to be good judgment; because certainly the proposals we now have and which have been approved in my opinion are not a rejection or turning back on what was said originally in

August, but are an improvement. This is a completely new proposal which has been strengthened and certainly guarantees the rights and needs of Canada much better than the first one ever did. The changes are substantial; you cannot overlook them, but the resulting proposition which we have had outlined to us by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in my opinion represents a very sound basis so far as Canada is concerned.
The present northern pipe line must remain as the main transmission line for Canadian gas. This is what the proposal guarantees. As the market in eastern and northern Canada develop, this pipe line is to be twinned. Assurance has been given by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines that the looping of the present line will begin by 1970 and be completed as the markets demand. What can be more sensible than this? What is the use of building it before it is necessary, so long as we have the guarantee that it will be done when it is required?
The requirements that are demanded of the Great Lakes Transmission Company, so far as the volume guarantees are concerned, are likewise sound, because this does guarantee a certain flow of gas on the new line but still retains the northern line as the main line so far as the volume which reaches eastern Canada is concerned.
So, although gas is guaranteed for any development in northern Ontario or eastern Canada, there are some outstanding benefits inherent in this proposal which were not contained in the original proposal. I think eastern Canada should take very close cognizance of these benefits.
The price of gas to eastern Canadian markets will be reduced because the cost of construction of the line will be less, and because the extra size of the line is going to be used up in meeting the needs of the available export markets in central and northern United States. This tremendous potential in the United States market is something to which we should not close our eyes. Our balance of trade deficit with the United States this year is more than $1 billion. speechtext: I have a question for the Secretary of State. speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of State):
subtopic: CHARLOTTETOWN, P.E.I.-FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR MEMORIAL BUILDING
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister announced last night, I think, that the federal government is increasing its grant to the confederation centre at Charlottetown. The house will know that no provision was made for any operating assistance by the federal government when the centre was conceived and erected. Since that time it has been supported partly by an annual federal grant of roughly $100,000 and partly by large contributions, considering the population of the island, by the province of Prince Edward Island, as well as substantial contributions by individuals who were interested.
Recently the trustees found they had come to the end of these resources and made a plea to the federal government to increase its assistance. Under my immediate predecessor there had been for one year an increase in the grant to $150,000. It became apparent that the $100,000 annual grant was not going to be sufficient so the Prime Minister announced that there would be an additional payment this year of another $100,000, making a total of $200,000 for this year to meet the immediate needs and assure the continued operation of the centre. All employees who have been given notice, I think for November 5, will not have to be discharged.
Then as a long term solution, since this is the only such centre in Canada and one which was constructed by federal and provincial funds from all the provinces, the federal government has made a very generous offer to pay a sum equivalent to one half of the deficits hereafter in perpetuity, but not to exceed $175,000 a year. It is hoped that this, together with the increasing sums to come in from those who are using the centre, both tourists and island residents, will assure the continued utilization of the centre on an increasing level to the benefit of the island and Canada as a whole.
October 28, 1966

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The house again in committee of supply, estimates of the Department of Labour for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1967. Shall vote No. 1, to be found at page 200 of the blue book, carry?

Mr. Chairman, since I first spoke on these estimates in late May some 20 members of the house have participated in discussions, some more than once. They have raised very interesting and some very important matters, and I should like to comment on some of them.
One line of thought, one constructive suggestion has been common to several of the speeches made in the house during this debate. I refer to expressions of opinion by the hon. members for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes, Red Deer, Halifax, Notre-Dame-de-Grace and Villeneuve, among others. They share concern as to whether there is enough serious research and advance analysis by the officials of the Department of Labour in order to prevent industrial disputes, as opposed to trying to settle them after the stoppage of work has occurred. I think the house and the Canadian public should have the advantage of this information.
It will be recalled that when the estimates first came before the house, on May 27 I think, a number of very serious strikes affecting the national economy were either in progress or on the eve of breaking out. Since then it may be recalled that parliament had to be especially convened to deal with the railway strike.
While these work disruptions resulting from unresolved labour disputes were of serious concern, I think it is important that members of this house should look at them in their proper perspective. It is interesting to note that in actual experience a relatively small percentage of labour disputes in Canada have ended in strikes or walk-outs. We wish that none had happened but, as I say, the
October 28, 1966

percentage of cases where work stoppage has occurred has been relatively small.
For the past fiscal year just prior to April 1 last, 103 disputes were referred to conciliation officers of my department, no less than 67 of those being settled with the help of those officers without even a conciliation board. Another 29 disputes were later settled by conciliation boards set up by my predecessor and by myself. In all, 90 out of 103 disputes during the last fiscal year were settled. This, I submit, is a creditable record.
Since April 1, 1966, the beginning of this fiscal year, 38 disputes have been settled as a result of the efforts of the departmental conciliation officers in Ottawa and in the field. Another 14 disputes have been settled by conciliation boards, and another four by special mediation efforts. At present 23 disputes are in the hands of conciliation officials or conciliation boards, and we hope these disputes will be amicably settled. One or two disputes are rather disturbing, but I hope that with the assistance of the trained officials and others who are engaged in the mediation process a solution will be found.
Will the minister allow the courtesy of a question at this stage?
Certainly.

Could the minister tell the committee how many man days were lost by reason of strikes in our country in 1965, also in 1966 to the latest date? The minister has that available, and I think it would be very helpful to know it. He is giving a most interesting dissertation on the subject matter to which he has devoted himself unceasingly, and I feel that this information would be most beneficial.

I thank the right hon. gentleman for his suggestion, which is a helpful one. I am sure my staff can readily provide that information, and it will be available within a very few minutes.

Could we have figures showing the amount of time lost as a result of accidents, illness and unemployment?

I am not sure that we shall be able to get those figures for the whole of Canada. We can undoubtedly give them fairly soon in respect of the field which comes within the federal domain. However, if they are available I am sure my officials will provide them before the discussion of these estimates concludes.

I have indicated that the development of further efforts to prevent work stoppages is a major matter of concern to us. This was a theme common to the remarks made by several hon. members. I wish to assure the committee that for the last several months we have been taking steps in the department to substantially strengthen our staff resources not only in Ottawa but elsewhere, and I am sure hon. members have read with interest of at least two or three of the appointments which have been made in the last few weeks.
I may say it has been clear to me almost from the day I took office as Minister of Labour that more attention must be paid to the basic issues which are raised in the course of the bargaining process. We must do a great deal more research. I believe it was the hon. member for Halifax and also the hon. member for Red Deer who put their fingers on this point. A great deal of work needs to be done so that more information will be available when crisis situations may arise. I may say that the department has made every effort to increase its sources of information so we may be kept abreast in this field, more particularly as to the effect technological changes have on bargaining negotiations. Such research involves looking into the whole question of technological change and its relation to employment. It also involves research into wages and productivity.
One of the most interesting things to have come out of our research in the last six months, at least in my opinion, is evidence of the grave discrimination which is to be found in the wage pattern in different parts of Canada. Many references have been made to the wage increase given to the longshoremen employed in the St. Lawrence ports. Very few people in this country know that within 90 days or so of that settlement increases, which were long overdue, had taken place in various parts of eastern Canada. One such increase went as high as 71 per cent over three years in order to bring the wages paid by that particular firm-and it was a sizeable firm-into line with what was being paid by other firms in the same industry in the province concerned.
I well remember the remark made by my parliamentary secretary when, in the course of the debate on these estimates, objection was taken by one hon. member to a 30 per cent increase-"Thirty per cent of what?" Mr. Chairman, 30 per cent of nothing is

October 28, 1968
Supply-Labour
nothing. If an industry or a firm is underpaying its employees, why should they not be brought to the level the circumstances warrant? The hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes, I think it was, referred to this point and I entirely endorse his remarks in this connection.
I do not wish to discuss, at this time, all the remarks which were made by the 20 members of the committee who took part in this debate at an earlier stage. Many of the points made were common to a number of the speeches; for example, the one to which I have just referred. One reason why I do not propose to do so is this. You will remember, Mr. Chairman, that on the three previous occasions when these estimates were before the committee we were in the midst of an atmosphere of strike. When the estimates were first considered the longshoremen's strike was in progress in Quebec. The second time they came up that strike was still in progress and an Air Canada strike was threatening. When the estimates came before the committee in June we were facing the possibility of the disruption of railway services. The reports of the first two conciliation boards were made public at about that time; at least the contents of those reports were disclosed at about that time. This is all behind us now, happily, and there is no necessity for me to deal with the comments which were made at that time, helpful and constructive though some of them were.
There are a few points in the debate, however, which might warrant special reference. First there is the matter raised yesterday by the hon. member for Lincoln, who referred to the automobile pact and its effect on employment in communities in Canada where the automobile industry is the major source of employment. I can only say that two of my colleagues and I have held one or more meetings-I have attended three-with representatives of the United Automobile Workers and with the mayor of the city of Oshawa and a delegation from that city, and that another meeting is to take place on Tuesday next when we hope further information will be available and we shall be able to discuss with the delegates some of the points which have arisen out of previous discussions. It is of the utmost importance that workers who are displaced-and there has been some displacement-through the operation of the automotive pact should be treated fairly by finding alternative employment and 
the provision of their just dues arising from TAB or any other form of assistance to which they may be entitled. I am hopeful that out of our discussions next week will come a solution to this particular problem.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Yesterday, as well as on an earlier occasion, the hon. member for York South stated that the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act had been found wanting, at least in certain fields. He referred particularly to disputes in the transportation field. Hon. members will perhaps recall that in my opening statement on May 27 I referred to this same fact and invited constructive suggestions from members of the committee by way of advice so that we might be able to apply in finding a solution for this very difficult problem. I may say it was because of the peculiar difficulties that seemed to be associated with national transportation-railways, air lines, other fields of transportation and allied activities, and in this connection I am thinking of the longshoremen on both coasts-that the Prime Minister, after consultation with his Minister of Labour and others, was prompted to establish the task force which was announced a few weeks ago, and which is to be headed by Dean Wood.
Last night the hon. member for York South put forward some suggestions. He was one of the few to do so. I am not saying they provide all the answers, but they merit consideration and will be referred to this task force for study. I share the hon. member's view that the government does not expect to find an answer to this problem within a few months. If the task force was going to work on the problem for only two or three months it would not have been appointed. This is a matter that should be studied in depth, and I am looking forward to a helpful report. Perhaps we will get a progress report within six months, but if the force is able to deal with it fully in such a relatively short time I shall be one of the most surprised men in Canada.
I would like to thank the hon. member for Comox-Alberni for his congratulations to the Minister of Labour and more particularly to the officials of the department for the part they played in arranging and conducting the I.L.O. regional conference in Ottawa in September.
The hon. member raised one point which I think merits an answer at this time. He drew attention to the problem connected with
October 28, 1966

statutory holidays. Under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code a certain number of statutory holidays are prescribed each year, and workers must be paid for those days whether they work or not. But if they do work, depending on their respective collective agreements they are to get time and a half or double time. However, the condition for receiving this time and a half or double time pay is that they must have worked 15 days during the previous month.
As most hon. members know, and as I certainly do after my experiences of the last three or four months, longshoremen work for a number of different employers. They may work for as many as four or five employers during the course of 15 days, and there was a serious legal question as to whether they would be covered under the act.
This question arose during negotiations between longshoremen and employers on the west coast, and in an exchange of telegrams later made public in the press if I remember correctly, I gave an assurance that if a solution could not be found in negotiations, as is done in other fields of endeavour where employees working for three or four firms qualify for unemployment insurance credits, at a very early date in this session I would cause a resolution to be placed on the order paper to deal with this matter. I repeat that assurance now, and the resolution will appear at a relatively early date, depending on our progress with the legislative program now before the house.
The same hon. member inquired about the progress being made by the industrial commissioner who was appointed to inquire into two issues that arose at the time of the settlement of the longshoremen's strike. These involved increased productivity, the possibility of reorganizing gangs, the size and use of slings and different other types of equipment, and job security.
Quite frankly I was disturbed and disappointed with the reports that I got during the first three or four weeks this inquiry was under way. At the outset the commissioner was confronted with a series of legal submissions, and objections were raised to his jurisdiction. However, I am happy to say that notwithstanding the fact that the first month or five weeks seemed to be taken up with this legal by-play, encouraging progress seems to have been made during the last several weeks. The longshoremen and their counsel are co-operating with the commissioner, and the inquiry is progressing satisfactorily.

The hon. member for Lapointe, and later on the hon. member for Trois Rivieres, dealt with the jursidictional dispute, or rather the request for certification by one of the affiliates of the C.N.T.U. in connection with the activities of the C.B.C. A hearing took place on this matter, I think in or about December of last year, to which several unions were parties. The union affiliated with the C.N.T.U. first asked to be certified as the bargaining agent for French speaking employees in the province of Quebec, and later at the actual hearing amended their request to cover all the employees of the C.B.C. in Quebec.
This matter was considered at some length by the Canada Labour Relations Board and following precedents which it had built up over a period of 20 years, it decided that since C.B.C. activities were national in scope they were similar to those of railway and air line companies. On that ground it decided not to fragment the unions on the matter of bargaining. After all, the idea of bargaining is to try to get the best possible terms for employees, and the board felt it was more appropriate that the bargaining should be conducted by an organization that is national in scope rather than a regional organization.

views ot these organizations have been heard and briefs are being considered by a committee of cabinet. I should now like to give the information that was requested by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition concerning the number of strikes and walk-outs and the number of days that were lost in the last five or six years. I have that information before me. I will have to give the figures for this year by months. I have the figures for the first eight months. Before the minister finishes, Mr. Chairman, would he deal briefly with the question raised by the hon. member for York South last night? What about injunctions in general, Mr. Chairman? I am not going to repeat the very reasoned arguments advanced by the hon. member for York South. It may be that the minister will disagree with me, but I believe there is no room at all for the use of injunctions in labour disputes. I am not a lawyer and it may be that I do not realize all the ramifications, but I believe that if there is difficulty on the picket line, if a picketer breaks a law or intimidates somebody, if a picketer uses violence against somebody, we do not need an injunction because he can be charged under the Criminal Code.
I say, therefore, that I see no useful purpose being served in labour disputes by injunctions. However, even if the minister and the government do not agree, why could the government not introduce very soon the kind of legislation recommended in the most practical and very moderate suggestions made by the hon. member for York South? I do not want to be critical or use unparliamentary language, but I suggest it is no accident that none of the judges in our courts have had much experience with labour-management relations. Most of them have a great deal more experience in corporation law than they have in labour matters. And we know it because Mr. Jodoin does not hesitate to hold press conferences to say that the negotiation unit must be interpreted as it is now because it suits the labour union which he has been representing for many years and because he is aware also that this is choking the rival labour unions, the C.N.T.U. for instance.
As Mr. Claude Ryan put it so well, the membership of the Labour Relations Board constitutes a real denial of justice when the members are called upon to make a decision.
Therefore, the interpretation of negotiation unit which appears in section 2 (3) should be redefined. The membership and structure of the Canada Labour Relations Board should also be revised.
I am asking the minister to be kind enough to consider those claims. He should not wait for the conflict to get worse. We have met federal members from Quebec belonging to all parties. Last Tuesday evening, the C.N.T.U. officials were accompanied by other radio and television people, and we could feel that this particular trade union was suffering deeply. And when these officials had threatened a few days earlier to withdraw from federal organizations, if justice was not rendered according to their claims, we sincerely believed that they would make good their threat.
This, to my mind, would be a backward step for Canadian workers' vital interests as well as for federal employees, and also a backward step in the national union and good harmony which must be encouraged and furthered in this country.
In the labour field, as in many other areas, cultural duality comes to the surface, it comes so much to light that when the C.N.T.U. representing a group of employees on the French network of C.B.C., was not granted union recognition by the Canada Labour Relations Board, the Montreal employees of the French network, together with labour leaders of the C.N.T.U., whom we well know, realized they would enjoy greater security and could better improve their working conditions, in accordance with their culture, by adhering to the C.N.T.U. labour union rather than to the national union and,
Supply-Labour
thus being affiliated to international unions who were not much concerned about or, probably, not at all interested in the duality of cultures and particular problems arising in the province of Quebec, which is a province different from the others, not only from the economic and administrative point of view, but from the labour view point, where culture and language at work are concerned.
Those who sat on the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, and who had the opportunity to ask numerous questions to witnesses who appeared, Mr. Ouimet, among others, when he was president of the C.B.C. received answers which brought out the fact that, for similar programs, on the French and the English networks, more money was spent on the English network than on the French network. And we were given the opportunity, while meeting with employees of the C.B.C. French network in Montreal, to realize the problems they had to face as French Canadians and employees of the C.B.C. Well, it is this attitude which the C.N.T.U. reflected. And the C.L.R.B. still refuses to grant it the right to negotiate for these people.
I hope the hon. minister, at the very beginning of next week, now that the ministerial committee has received the documents, and translation of a certain number of other documents, will use its influence-

As reported at page 9211 of Hansard, about the middle of the first column, I was making some reference to a situation involving the International Longshoremen's and Warehousemen's Union. Commencing at that point in my remarks I would like to repeat something of what I said last night. What I did say was along these lines: Earlier this year some of the members of that union went to

jail because they refused to work on a statutory holiday as prescribed by the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. In view of the obscurity so far as the words relating to the definition of employer are concerned, I think some explanation should be given at this time as to what changes in the law the government has in mind to prevent a recurrence of this situation.
It is my understanding that the minister at one time assured us that if this matter was not resolved through a process of collective bargaining he would take it upon himself to bring in, for the consideration of parliament, amendments to the code to alleviate this situation. It would be beneficial if we received some progress report in this regard from the minister.
I should also like to hear from the minister a progress report on what he described as a taskforce operating under the leadership of Dean Woods of McGill University. For a long time, certainly since before the present minister assumed office, we have been told that proposed amendments to the present Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act have been under consideration. Surely by now the minister can tell us when the government will have proposals ready to place before parliament.
When the minister is replying on this matter perhaps he can relate his comments to the suggestions made earlier by the hon. member for York South concerning special railway and transport labour legislation.
Having made those comments or corrections, Mr. Chairman, before I resume my seat I would also like to suggest to the minister my own personal view that his estimates for next year might perhaps be profitably referred to the committee on labour and employment so that a study of the estimates can

be made of a somewhat different nature than has been possible during this calendar year, which I am sure most of us will agree has been a rather turbulent one in his department. I am sure we all hope that next year we may have a suitable opportunity to enter into a more detailed study of the operations of his department such as could be given in a standing committee. It would serve to increase our understanding and perhaps produce some useful suggestions from members as to how operations of his department might be more profitable in the future.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, we all can benefit from experience. I most certainly agree, this being the fifth or sixth occasion that we have had on these estimates, that it might be more profitable to refer them to the committee. I also share the hon. member's hope that labour-management relations will be in a little quieter tempo next year than they were this year.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday I spoke about the problem raised and created by the Canada Labour Relations Board which deprived some workers, some citizens of Quebec and Canada of their freedom to choose their own representation and bargaining unit.
Well, I have here a news release from the Department of Labour, No. 6475, dated October 21, 1966, and entitled: "Canada Labour Relations Board orders representation vote by C.B.C. production employees". Those are the employees who, at the end of 1965 or the beginning of 1966, asked the Canada Labour Relations Board to allow them to change their bargaining union and give their allegiance to a new labour union which, at that time, was affiliated to the C.N.T.U.
I will now read the news release, Mr. Chairman, because I think that it should be put on record to prove the bad faith of the Canada Labour Relations Board in that particular case. I quote:
The Minister of Labour, Honourable John R. Nicholson, announced today that the Canada Labour Relations Board has ordered that a representation vote be taken of certain employees of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at various centres across Canada who are affected by an application for certification made to the Board by the Canadian Union of Public Employees.
October 28, 1966

It is the Canadian union of public employees that asked for a vote on the matter of representation. I will now resume reading the news release:
The Board directed that the names of the applicant union and also the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees and Moving Picture Machine Operators of the United States and Canada,
Known as the I.A.T.S.E.
which presently holds a collective agreement with the C.B.C. covering the employees in the bargaining unit involved, should appear on the ballot.
The board requested that the names of those two unions, that is the one which is asking to represent the C.B.C. employees and the I.A.T.S.E. which formerly represented the C.B.C. employees, be entered on the ballot.
I now resume reading the news release:
The decision of the board followed a two-day public hearing of the parties concerned on September 7 and 8, 1966, during which the Board received evidence and argument put forward by the two unions whose names will appear on the ballot, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as the respondent employer, and also two other intervening unions. Syndicate general du cinema et de la television (C.N.T.U.), and the Canadian Wire Service Guild Local 213 of the American Newspaper Guild.
I will come back to the news release a little later. Right now I would like to point out that the union affiliated to the C.N.T.U. is not allowed to have its name on the ballot. The C.B.C. employees are not allowed to choose between all the competing unions, especially when the Syndicat general du cinema et de la t&evision, affiliated to the C.N.T.U., indicated on behalf of the C.B.C. employees, about ten months ago or so, that they wanted to be represented precisely by the S.G.C.T. affiliated to the C.N.T.U.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that there is bad faith and something abnormal in this case.
Here is another quotation from that news release:
The application affected 1,584 employees of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Of these 1,200 are employed in Montreal and Toronto, and the remainder at nine locations from Vancouver, B.C., to Corner Brook and St. John's, Nfld. The group consists of production employees employed in 53 job classifications including such classifications as set designer, graphic designer, carpenter, painter, film editor, film cameraman, make-up artist, costume designer, seamstress, film librarian, and stagehand.
Mr. Chairman, there are 1,584 employees within the C.B.C. in the various categories I have just mentioned in the news release, some of them working for the French network and some for the English network.
Supply-Labour
As was so well mentioned by those I quoted, namely Gerard Pelletier, responsible for an article in the January 26, 1966 issue of the Montreal Star, and Jean-Marc Leger, in an editorial in Le Devoir of January 24, 1966, there are social and cultural differences between the French network employees and those of the English network. I quoted from articles of those two gentlemen, one of which is a full-time journalist, and the other less so, to the effect that there are regional, social and cultural differences between the two networks.
And yet the Canada Labour Relations Board insists on denying the employees of the C.B.C. French network the right to choose their union freely, and this is shown once more in the press release of the Department of Labour dated October 21, 1966, which I have just quoted.
Several months ago, on the insistence of the C.B.C. employees, the C.N.T.U. asked to represent them as bargaining agent. The vote of the employees was rejected at that time. They were plainly dissatisfied with their union. Another body, the Canadian Union of Public Employees, sent to the Canada Labour Relations Board a request for certification as bargaining agent of the C.B.C. employees. Since the C.B.C. employees were still dissatisfied with their former union, I.A.T.S.E., the Canada Labour Relations Board ordered a representation vote to be taken among C.B.C. production employees, the very same workers who, ten months earlier, had been refused permission to choose a new union because it was affiliated to the C.N.T.U. Today, they have now been allowed to do so, because this is another union, but affiliated to the C.L.C. in the same way as I.A.T.S.E.
Mr. Chairman, I feel, and you will undoubtedly agree with me, that this is completely out of keeping with union freedom. Does freedom for the employees to choose their own union mean that they are free to choose only among those unions affiliated to the C.L.C. and that they will no longer be free to choose among unions affiliated to the C.N.T.U.? I am not against the C.L.C. in any way; no. All I want to do is stand up for union freedom and freedom of choice for the workers, whatever their trade or their field of endeavour. They should be free to choose their union.
I am not favouring the C.N.T.U. over the C.L.C. Not at all. I am standing up for the C.B.C. employee, who must be left free to choose his own negotiating unit, whether it

October 28/ 196&
Supply-Labour
be a C.L.C. unit or a C.N.T.U. unit. In the present case, the C.B.C. employee is not free to choose, since only two names are allowed to appear on the ballot, namely, the Canadian Union of Public Employees and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees. These are the only two names permitted. And even though the Syndicat general du cinema et de la television affiliated to the C.N.T.U. made the same request on two occasions to the Canada Labour Relations Board, the name of the Syndicat general du cinema et de la Television is not allowed on the ballot.
Mr. Chairman, we wish to protest against such a situation. The minister admitted a while ago that the C.N.T.U. had voiced some protests following the decision by the Canada Labour Relations Board and he stated that following these protests, a committee headed by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) had been set up within the cabinet to study the question. Several times during the last few months, we have asked the committee if it was ready to report on its study sessions. The committee appointed by the cabinet has been studying the problem for eight months.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise a question of privilege affecting the rights and privileges of every member of this house. As is well known, under the rules the discussion of estimates and supply motions is limited to a very few days. There are 265 members of th's house and each one of them is entitled to the opportunity to take part in this discussion. I have raised no objection to the hon. member for Lapointe talking as often as he likes, but when he is now repeating the same arguments that he advanced at length last night on two different occasions I submit that he is abusing the privileges of members of this house.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Labour has just said that I spoke yesterday on two occasions. That is not exactly in accordance with the facts, because I spoke only on one occasion; the other time it was on a question of privilege, in order to rectify some erronous translation given by the Chair. Therefore, I shall ask the Minister of Labour not to mislead this house by saying that I spoke on two occasions. Yesterday, I only

spoke on one occasion on the subject and I shall ask the Minister of Labour to correct his statement so as not to mislead the house. Besides, he just has to check in yesterday's Hansard to realize that I am strictly telling the truth.
Now, I am not repeating what I said yesterday, I am only following up the argument mentioned at noon by the Minister of Labour following my intervention yesterday, and I am just coming to that after a summary of new developments, mainly the press release of the Minister of Labour that was published recently and that I did not have in hand yesterday, since I obtained it only this morning, and after hearing the Minister of Labour answer the arguments I put forward yesterday, I am simply coming back to that.
In my opinion, the Minister of Labour would be very ill-advised to suggest that I am delaying uselessly the business of the house, because I am certainly not the one to have taken up most of the 52 hours allowed for the study of the estimates of various departments.
As I was saying, the Minister of Labour told us this afternoon that the committee set up by the cabinet would submit its report shortly. Well, I say to the minister that we have been expecting that report for the past eight months without getting it. If the ministerial committee appointed to look fully into-the matter raised today, namely that the Canada Labour Relations Board may have flouted the union freedom of Quebec workers, can wait eight months before correcting that situation, I feel that members of the house can take at least one day to protest against the activities of Canada Labour Relations Board and also against the slowness of the minister and of the committee appointed to inquire into the fact that the union freedom of workers is being flouted. If the minister can take eight months to consider such a problem, I feel a member can take one hour to protest against the incomprehensible and unjustifiable slowness of the ministers in looking into a problem involving union freedom and individual freedom.
Mr. Chairman, I moved an amendment yesterday. Besides, the minister told us, I believe, that the cabinet committee was expected to submit its report shortly. I say, therefore, that the estimates of the Department of Labour should not be passed until the committee of ministers has reported on the problem now being raised in the house.
October 28, 1966

Those estimates, and especially item one, should not be passed as long as the ministerial committee set up to study that problem has not submitted its report.
Why? Because the first item precisely reads as follows:
Administration of the Industrial Relations Act.
And it is precisely under this legislation that the Canada Labour Relations Board operates and that it will cost the Canadian taxpayer in 1966-67 the total amonut of $594,900, with the salaries of officials and administrators accounting for $367,000.
Well, Mr. Chairman, if an item of $594,900 is passed to enable the Canada Labour Relations Board to encroach upon the rights of Canadian workers, then I say that it is the right, the duty and not only the privilege of any member of this house to protest and refuse to vote the necessary estimates for the operation of this Canada Labour Relations Board, if this Board uses public funds to encroach upon the union freedom of the people.
Mr. Chairman, this amount is included in item No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Labour and 1 want to protest against the fact that today an amount of $594,900 will be passed to pay for the expenses of the Canada Labour Relations Board.
On the contrary, I believe those estimates should stand and should not be approved before the cabinet committee, appointed especially to deal with this problem, reports on it. And that is the reason why I should like to present a motion similar to that of yesterday, but which is in order this time. Unfortunately, my motion is in French only and hand-written; I have no copy, since an adequate staff is not always available when it is necessary to get such things done quickly. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe):
That the amount mentioned in vote No. 1 under the item "Administration of the Industrial Relations Act" be reduced to $1.
The purpose of the amendment, Mr. Chairman, is not too reduce the salary of the hon. minister to $1, not to reduce the other amounts in vote No 1 to $1, but merely the amounts mentioned under the item "Administration of the Industrial Relations Act". Its purpose is precisely to implement this act governing the Canada Labour Relations Board and I do not believe we should vote an amount of $594,900 for the Canada Labour
Supply-Labour
Relations Board. I even believe $1 is too much for what this Canada Labour Relations Board has done.
Mr. Chairman, I know the question is being considered by the ministerial committee, but I feel that this committee has delayed enough already. We have just learned from the hon. minister that the report of the committee is about to be tabled. But nevertheless, as I said before, I do not think that we will be able to pass the item that I wish to have reduced at the present time, before the ministerial committee tables its report.
In concluding my comments, I would simply say that the ministerial committee is still considering the situation and I would like to refer its members to two paragraphs of a brief presented to the committee by the C.N.T.U. Paragraph 34 reads as follows:
It is unbelievable that the Canadian parliament would appoint such an organization (C.L.R.B.) whose aim it would be to grant privileges to one union.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
It is unthinkable that the federal cabinet would remain a helpless witness to such a glaring violation of the right of association: it is unthinkable that the cabinet would be helpless before such a staggering inconsistency.
And in paragraph 35, I also wish to quote the following sentence:
Judicial equality before the law cannot be denied. Groups of workers cannot be forced to become members of decaying unions, under the pretext that they are established "coast to coast".
I will end my comments by quoting Marcel Pepin, general president of the C.N.T.U., who says in the preface to a small booklet entitled "Trade Unionism and freedom at C.B.C.":
The French network of the C.B.C. is, for all practical purposes, established exclusively in Quebec. Employees of the French network, dissatisfied at being represented by a far-away union which is practically unknown to them, inefficient, unable to understand them, and unable to provide them with a framework wherein they can really express themselves, have decided to withdraw from the organization which holds them prisoners and join the C.N.T.U., which will give them the opportunity to run their own affairs.
So, they say to themselves, why could not a French network, which is for all practical purposes a distinct section from the standpoint of language, working procedures, administration, geographical situation, personnel, concentration of manpower in one area of the country, why could it not be considered as an appropriate negotiation unit? No answers the C.L.R.B. It would be in accordance with reason, the workers' will, and the principle of union freedom, but the Canada Labour Relations Board (three to one) is against this.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I also thank the hon. member for Villeneuve for providing me with an opportunity to submit a few remarks on this amendment.
As was very ably explained by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), it is not so much a matter of reducing the minister's salary, but rather to emphasize the importance of the problem caused by labour relations between unions such as the C.N.T.U. and others, and the Canadian government and federal agencies.
This afternoon I had an opportunity to speak on item 1 of the estimates of the Department of Labour. I do not want to be redundant with the same remarks. However, I have just been informed that, in my Sherbrooke riding, a small group of union members who do not belong to the C.N.T.U. have presumedly raised a strong protest against the stand I took recently in the House of Commons, with regard to the grievances

raised by the C.N.T.U., and last Tuesday night, in room 112N, they came to meet the labour leaders of the C.N.T.U.
Well, I want to say that I am not at all interested, Mr. Chairman, in disputes between labour unions when I endorse the views and support the grievances presented by unions on matters of principle, on the freedom of the worker, on the individual freedom, on the fulfilment of the worker's right, which he exercises through any union whatsoever.
I want to say clearly in this house that I am not the defender of the C.N.T..U, the C.L.C. or the F.Q.W., no matter the initials. It is a matter of principle. And when we ask the Minister of Labour, again by this amendment, to speed up the studies and the business, and to amend section 2 (3) of the industrial relations and labour disputes act so as to define in detail a collective bargaining unit and to give us the size of a local and administrative extension, it is because the problem is urgent.
Evidently, we learned through the newspapers this morning that the representatives of the F.Q.W., the federation of Quebec workers, in response to the action taken by the C.N.T.U. this week, are supposed to come next Tuesday evening, I believe, to meet us, the federal members for Quebec. They will submit to us their views on Bill C-170 and other grievances. They will probably air their views on the unit of negotiation and will insist so that it is considered only from the national standpoint.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I should be delighted to attend that meeting in Room 112-N Tuesday evening. I hope to see there the few F.Q.W. union leaders who, while I was away from my constituency, denounced my anti-labour attitude in press releases, and wrongly so since I fight for the freedom of workers and am in no way interested in disputes between unions. I hope to see them in Room 112-N so that I can answer their charges properly.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I fail to see the connection of the hon. member's remarks with the amendment before the committee.

Here goes, Mr. Chairman. I greatly appreciate the interventions of the

hon. minister. When I spoke this afternoon, he interrupted me. He could not see how my speech tied in with my chiding of the Canada Labour Relations Board for failing to hold its deliberations in the two official languages, of the government for not taking into consideration, when appointing members to the Board, of our dual culture, and for not appointing bilingual members. The hon. minister could not see the connection when I spoke of a federal agency under the Department of Labour.
Again, in my comments on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lapointe, and dealing precisely with the union grievances with regard to the Canada Labour Relations Board, the hon. minister fails to see the relation with the present debate.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that one of the two of us suffers from intellectual myopia in addition to the physical myopia which afflicts us both.
I am of the opinion, Mr. Chairman, that I am not out of order in my comments and in supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Lapointe.

Mr. Chairman, I shall have to make a few remarks about various subjects regarding the item in the estimates of the Minister of Labour, under consideration at this time.
I fully agree with those in favour of freedom for the union people to join a union of their choice. I share 100 per cent their views and I shall not enlarge on this subject because I fully agree with the remarks made by those who have discussed that subject.
I should like to deal with another question, that of the unemployment insurance offices. Some unemployment insurance offices have to be moved. In the area where I come from-

Mr. Chairman, I want to say just a few words on this amendment intended to reduce to $1 vote No. 1 of the department of Labour. This amendment is the result of the dilatory tactics of the department and of the ministers who are on the committee which is looking into the union problem within the federal civil service. Mr. Chairman, if I disagree with the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), it is because of a problem between the C.N.T.U., the Q.L.F., the C.N.P.U. and the C.C.R.O. This is not a problem for the ministers to settle. The unions should try to get along with one another. In my opinion, the minister, the ministers and the government would not object to the bargaining unit. And I think that the way to get to the bargaining unit, while respecting the right of association of everybody, would be for the unions to try to reach an agreement between themselves. As soon as these unions have reached such an agreement to set up a bargaining unit with the employer, that is the federal government, then the hon. member for Lapointe will have no reason to move an amendment intended to reduce to $1 item No. 1 of the department of Labour.
I disagree with the hon. member for Lapointe in that respect and I will certainly vote against the amendment he moved because I would have preferred an amendment suggesting to the various unions in Canada to start getting along with one another before requesting the government's intervention.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, it is unfortunate that I have not many copies of my amendment, because I would have sent one to the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). I think he did not understand the amendment I have moved.
He did not receive it, and my amendment is exactly the contrary of what the hon. member for Villeneuve just mentioned. I rise only to inform him. I did not propose to reduce item No. 1 to $1, but I proposed to reduce, within item No. 1, only the part in which subsidies are granted to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, in the amount of $594,900, while the total amount of item No. 1 is $4,539,100. Now, I do not suggest that this amount be reduced to $1, but

October 28, 1966
Supply-Labour
only that portion of the item respecting the administration of the Industrial Relations Act. And the reason I pick out this particular item is because these amounts allow the Canada Labour Relations Board to operate. This amount is allotted to the Canada Labour Relations Board.
Now, I would like to explain why I have reduced only this amount to $1 in my amendment. It is, because this problem has not been raised by the unions, by the workers, or by the minister but by the Canadian Labour Relations Board. And today, the unions can no longer solve it, the minister has to solve it, because he is responsible for the Canadian Labour Relations Board which gave rise to that problem.
The member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) said that the minister did not have to solve this problem, but that the unions should reach an agreement among themselves.
It is true that it is always better when the unions can agree. But, here, in the case involved, the employees of the C.B.C. were members of a union called:	International
Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees and Moving Picture Machine Operators of the United States and Canada. Their business agent was far from the C.B.C. employees in Montreal; he did not take care of their interests and did not remain in contact with them, as was said by the employees themselves, They received letters in English and, if they answered in French, their letters were returned with a note asking them to write in English. When it was time for the C.B.C. employees to sign a new contract, two years ago, I believe, it had to go through the International Alliance of United States and Canada, whereas the C.B.C. employees had prepared a contract in French, to be signed with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The contract was translated into English, and badly, by this agent who lives far from Quebec. There were mistakes in translation exactly like the one which occurred last night, when I introduced an amendment. The contract was signed with the mistakes left in the English version. This was the last straw, and the C.B.C. workers told us: We no longer want to belong to the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees and Moving Picture Machine Operators of the United States and Canada.
Then the C.B.C. employees applied to the C.N.T.U., formed a union called Syndicat general du Cinema et de la Television, and asked it to represent them. The new union
[Mr. Gregoire.i
said: fine; we will see whether we can find enough members among you who want to leave the American union and join us, and if there are enough, we will send a request to the Canada Labour Relations Board. The majority of C.B.C. employees voted in favour of this.
The C.N.T.U. then appeared before the board, which refused its request saying that it did not allow the Syndicat general du Cinema et de la Television to represent the C.B.C. employees. Therefore there was no vote. The C.N.T.U. protested that the employees were still dissatisfied and had requested another vote. Another union then contacted them, the Canadian Union of Public Employees. The C.B.C. employees were told: we can represent you, we are also affiliated to the C.L.C.
On October 21, the Canada Labour Relations Board allowed the C.B.C. employees to vote, but insisted that only two names appear on the voting paper, the Canadian Union of Public Employees and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees and Moving Picture Machine Operators of the United States and Canada. The C.N.T.U. tried to get its name on the voting paper, but its request was denied. This meant that the Syndicat general du Cin6ma et de la T616-vision, affiliated to the C.N.T.U., was excluded from the vote.
Therefore, the problem there was not created by a misunderstanding among the unions, or by the minister. It will not be solved by improved relations between the unions. The law says that for a vote to be taken, for the employees to choose their own union, the vote must be approved by the Canada Labour Relations Board, and in this connection the Board rejected the request of the C.B.C. employees.
What else can we do? Who must be blamed? The unions, no. They have done their best, at least the C.N.T.U. The C.L.C. is doing its best under the circumstances. The minister? The problem has been laid on his door-step, and he must settle it. The problem is so acute that a committee of seven ministers has been set up to deal with it. But who must be blamed? Who has posed the problem? It is the Canada Labour Relations Board.
It is for that reason and after those explanations that I said to the member for Villeneuve that I would like to see him vote with us on that amendment. I told him that the purpose of the amendment was not to
-October 28, 1966

reduce the total amount of item No. 1 of the Department of Labour, but only a part of it, that is about 10 per cent of the item. The whole Department of Labour's estimates amount to $10,513,400, item No. 1 amounting to $4,569,100. We cannot reduce everything. The only detail involved and that is mentioned in the amendment, is that concerning the application of the Industrial Relations Act; the Canada Labour Relations Board is responsible for the problem.
1 say that those who are responsible for that problem do not deserve $594,900; hence, I ask that it be reduced to $1. When the minister comes back with the report of the cabinet committee, presided over by the hon. Mr. Winters, if the decision is right and if the Canada Labour Relations Board wants to comply with it, then I will not object to the item being re-introduced. But that could not be done unless the adoption of the items is postponed until after the cabinet's decision and as the procedure does not allow me to do that, I take the means available to me under the procedure. I ask that that detail only and not all item No. 1 be reduced to $1. I ask this for the reasons I just outlined to the member for Villeneuve, and I hope I did so in all sincerity after giving him all the facts.
I hope he will agree with us that the Canada Labour Relations Board acted wrongly when it decided to deprive the General Union of the cinema and television affiliated to the C.N.T.U., as well as C.B.C. employees, of the freedom to choose their bargaining unit. If it acted wrongly, it would not be normal to vote once more an item of $594,000 for its sole purposes but that this amount be reduced to $1 until they mend its ways.

are rather elaborate and certainly mean something. The hon. minister must realize the importance of the matter, that is, what the reasons were for the denial of C.N.T.U. when the vote was taken allowing the C.B.C. employees to choose their union.
I now understand, partly as a result of what the hon. member for Lapointe said, that the two unions the member for Lapointe just named must have protested or exerted pressure upon the Canada Labour Relations Board so that the C.N.T..U would not be accepted. Allow me, Mr. Chairman, to explain something about the last point brought up by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). The Canada Labour Relations Board is made up of nine members, namely a chairman appointed by the Department of Labour, four employer representatives who are not government appointees, and four labour representatives. Now, of the four labour representatives three are delegated by the C.L.C. and one by the C.N.T.U. Inevitably, they disagree, three against one-
Who chose them?

It is the government and the Department of Labour who ask the C.L.C. to appoint three members and the C.N.T.U. to appoint one. When it is time to make decisions, one union is represented by three members and the other by only one. Even though they wanted to agree, the most powerful union, the one with three members on the Board, does not have to agree with the smaller union which has only one representative. It only has to make the decision which is carried by three votes to one. It is as simple as that.
Is it a fight between unions?

It is a fight between unions, but I do not call that a fight when it is a majority vote by three to one. It is no longer a fight but it can give rise to strife. The manner in which the Canada Labour Relations Board makes its decisions results in strife, which is quite understandable since

October 28, 1966
Supply-Labour
three of its members represent a union and only one represents the other. The more powerful is then easily tempted to get the better of the smaller one and say: "Let us vote, we are three". And they win the vote. A board was therefore established, the Canada Labour Relations Board, wherein are to be found all the seeds of disagreement. It is precisely the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, embodied by the Canada Labour Relations Board, which is fundamentally wrong and has given rise to disagreement and wrangling. That is what we cannot stand and that is why we are asking that the amount of $594,000 appropriated to that item be reduced to $1.
Mr. Chairman, I would like the member for Villeneuve to admit that if the cause for disagreement were removed from the Canada Labour Relations Board, there would be less strife and wrangling between the unions themselves. By reducing the item to $1, it may be possible to eliminate that cause for disagreement and wrangling between those two unions.

Mr. Chairman, I must remind the member for Lapointe that even though the Canada Labour Relations Board asks a large union to appoint three members and the C.N.T.U. to appoint one, the total number of members belonging to either union must be taken into account.
If the C.L.C. has five times more members than the C.N.T.U., it seems quite normal to me that there should be more representatives of the C.L.C. than of the C.N.T.U. within the organization; it seems to me that it is perfectly democratic. But the fact remains that the labour unions or the labour leaders should start by agreeing among themselves and if the principle of labour unionism becomes blurred, that is when the quarrelling begins. Even if there are five against three, or five against one, if they really understood the aims of labour unionism, we would not witness the quarrels which are at the bottom of what we are discussing now.

It is true that the C.L.C. has five times more members or almost than the C.N.T.U.; that they should have proportionally the same number of members on the Canada Labour Relations Board, that is fine, but when that board which has three C.L.C. members because its membership is larger and one C.N.T.U. member because it is smaller, is asked to decide whether or not the C.B.C. employees can choose their own labour

union, then the dice are loaded; those employees go to the Labour Relations Board and say: "We want a ballot", because they want to be represented by the C.N.T.U. The C.L.C., represented by three members, says no. It has a membership in Canada of 1,200,000 while the C.N.T.U. has only 200,000 members. Therefore, the employees of the C.B.C. do not have the right to join the small unions. They are voted down three to one, so they are forced to join the larger union.
Would you call that good representation? The member for Villeneuve cannot accept it. It is that principle that I object to: to have a Canada Labour Relations Board with labour representatives, in a greater number to represent the C.L.C. than the C.N.T.U. because the C.L.C. represents more workers than the C.N.T.U., without that board being left free to decide and to judge which union will represent such and such groups of employees; that is what I cannot accept.
And I think that the member for Villeneuve will not accept the fact that the majority, on account of its greater number of people, may select the representatives of another group.

When the minister answered my question regarding unemployment insurance for agricultural labour he said his department is now working on the necessary regulations and it is hoped to make them public at an early date. Mr. Chairman, I suppose the minister was making a realistic statement when he indicated that the chances of getting legislation to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act at this session are not very great. I would remind him, however, that his predecessor, during the first session that the present government was in power, expressed

the hope-it was almost a promise-that we would get such legislation in the following year. It seems we must keep waiting for things of this sort from year to year.
However, I should like to ask the minister whether the report to which he referred is available to hon. members. I suppose his answer will be that this is an interdepartmental report and that it is for the government only. But one can always hope that the unusual will happen. In any case, may I ask the minister a question with respect to one aspect of unemployment insurance. In doing so, I express the hope that this is one of the matters which may be dealt with by the proposed amendments.
I refer to the many unhappy situations which arise when recipients of unemployment insurance benefits are called in for investigation and inquiry as to their availability for employment. I am sure my experience is matched by that of most hon. members. Many people in these circumstances give what they think are honest and straightforward answers and many have in mind what they believe to be their rights. Then they discover that because they have indicated they are not prepared to work for considerably less, say, than they were getting when they were last on the job, they are declared to have restricted then-availability for employment and their benefits are cut off.
In some cases we are able to get cases reviewed. But it seems to me there are too many cases of this kind, too many situations in which people are trapped, to use a strong word, into making statements which result in their being disqualified from benefits. This has been going on for some time, not only under this government but under the previous one. I had hoped the practice was waning, but a few cases have come to my notice just recently.
It seems to me that if people make themselves available and are prepared to answer questions directly they should not be penalized in the way in which many people, to my knowledge, have been penalized. May I put this direct question to the minister: is this one of the subjects dealt with in the report to which he referred? Is this one of the subjects which may be dealt with in the amendments to the act?

In answer to the first question put to me, let me say that the report in question was prepared primarily for the information of the Minister of Labour, though

it was expected it would go on to the cabinet generally-and it will. But I am afraid that, having been prepared with that end in view, it is not one that can be made public, because views that are pro and con are put forward, as the hon. member might expect.

I shall ask the minister whether it would be possible to improve the situation of the unemployed while allowing them to work on farms, the farmers being in urgent need of help but deprived of the money necessary to pay the salaries asked by labour at the present time. Many farmers need manpower. In an area like the one in which I live, there are many unemployed, almost the whole year round, and the farmers are unable to hire them; they refuse to work for a few days, because they are afraid to lose the unemployment insurance payments and because they have to go through red tape to get registered again for unemployment insurance benefits.
Agriculture is in a state of stagnation and farmers need some hired help, but they are unable to pay for it. I would ask the minister whether it would not be possible to authorize the unemployed to go and work for farmers while they are receiving their unemployment insurance and the farmer could make up the difference. It would render a great service to agriculture and to farmers. This request has been made in various several places and by many farmers of my constituency. I ask the minister to take it into consideration.
Let us take, for example, the maple sugar operations in springtime. Many farmers need some hired help, because their income is not

high enough to pay full wages to those labourers. And a great number of unemployed could work, but since it is only for a few days, they do not do so, for fear of losing their insurance.

Now, some protests have been made to me in connection with the moving of the unemployment office from Megantic. I am asking the minister to take this matter into serious consideration. I live in a designated area. There is a large number of unemployed in our area. Some citizens are now compelled to travel 75 to 100 miles to go to the unemployment office. We have empty homes and their number is increasing. All those employed by the Unemployment Insurance Commission will also have to move to keep their jobs. Also, Mr. Chairman, in our area as well as in many others, but especially in ours, the municipality has gone to considerable expense to set up a decent unemployment insurance office. The municipality needs its funds, and if the office is moved, this means an enormous loss for us, and the municipality cannot think of any other citizens or institutions that could occupy these premises and pay the rent they ask. These things are not right and they bring about losses for the municipality and the area.
Now, we speak of decentralizing industry, but we are doing exactly the opposite, Mr. Chairman. We resort to centralization everywhere. When a new industry must be established somewhere, well, we centralize it. It is located in large communities. We have not had the opportunity to benefit by any new industry being established in our community for many years; and there are even some that are moving into other areas. Some small industries of our area are moving to larger centres because it is more beneficial for them.
Now, I do believe that the unemployment insurance office should remain where it is for the good of the population of the county and

the region, because we cannot afford to lose it, as this would be disastrous for the region and the municipality.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we centralize and move everything into large centres, to the detriment of smaller communities. I believe that this policy might have some advantages, but it also has disadvantages.
Centralization, Mr. Chairman, is what we have been doing for several years, but the time has come to consider the situation in a region such as that where I come from, particularly when we have something useful.
