In small communities, when a man goes into the office to look for work and register for benefits, these agencies should work in conjunction with each other. I have always been surprised to find the employment service saying, "John Doe is not registered with us" when he was in fact collecting benefit. I have not been able to understand how this difficulty could arise when both agencies were in the same building, and in fact in the same office. I could see no reason why, when a man registered for benefits he was not also registered for work. Some people know there is no work in that particular area and have a better understanding of the employment picture than others. But it seemed to me to be advantageous for people drawing unemployment assistance benefits to be able to register for and find work in the same locality.
We have seen this situation change over a period of time, and the division between

these two government agencies is such that the authorities have put a set of filing cabinets in the middle of the room to divide the two departments and have moved the employment section to the Department of Manpower and Immigration. This was not done because it was required by the Canadian people. It certainly was not required by those who used these offices. It was an administrative problem decided upon by the government themselves and certainly not by parliament. In many areas this system is not satisfactory.
I received a telephone call this afternoon from a young chap who told me that he knows of kick-backs and money being paid by government officials to private employment agencies. When I asked whether he could prove this, he said, "No, you will have to get the books of the government agencies, and even if you do you will probably find that these payments have been camouflaged in some way." He was interested in supplying me with names. I think there is a certain amount of manipulation going on in this area. I believe we have left ourselves wide open for this sort of thing. There is talk of the Civil Service Association disappearing and being replaced by the manpower centre, although we know that the manpower centre is not operating in respect of many industries.
In my area all the employers do their hiring through the National Employment Service offices and I believe we have established a very good relationship in this respect. In Ontario, particularly in northern Ontario, the department of highways have been hiring casual labourers through the Unemployment Insurance Commission offices. In most cases they have found employment for the guys who were drawing unemployment benefits from the government. This whole program could be interrelated in this way. It is a fact that if the federal government are going to employ Manpower Services, Office Overload and other agencies of this type on a temporary basis, rather than bringing in people on a permanent basis, there will be all kinds of abuses in this area. I think the government has taken a very retrograde step in deciding to separate the employment service from the unemployment insurance service. I believe that this separation lends itself to abuses.
I can remember as a young lad going for the first time to work in the mines. At that time you went to a private employment agency
October 28, 1966

and were immediately asked for $25 before the person in the agency would consider an application for a job in the mines. In those days the pay in the mines was 58 cents an hour. I did not pay the $25. I gave the guy a cock-and-bull story and told him that I owed a large sum of money to hotels, I had been out of the area where I had been working after Christmas-this was February-and owed so much money for hotels that if I did not get a job I would not be able to pay the hotels. These private employment agencies had all sorts of contacts with employers and for this reason expected a kick-back. But because I told him I owed money to hotels, he sent me for a job and I got it. Perhaps he expected a kick-back from the hotel.
The interesting thing about the situation was that I had only come to the area with my father a couple of days before, and obviously has just come off the farm. But I got the job without paying the money for which I was asked. In connection with private employment agencies in the Timmins area I know of cases where the person responsible for hiring workers had to have a bottle of whisky on the Saturday night or you did not have a job on the Monday morning.
If government agencies are going to hire Office Overload, for example, private deals will be conducted under the table. If parliament lends itself to this kind of thing we will have gone a long way back in the system which Canada has been able to develop under the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I agree with the minister that the act governing the commission was set up by parliament to solve many of the employment problems that we have in this country; but you cannot legitimately divorce unemployment from employment. If you do divorce these two things, you will find there is less connection between the people paying benefits and those supplying jobs than there has ever been in the past.
I should like to refer to a situation which exists in my area. For a few years we had a sub office established in the town of New Liskeard, which is 60 miles from Kirkland Lake where there is an unemployment insurance office. This office was able to solve almost every problem that came to me as a member of parliament. I had 15 or 20 complaints a week a few years ago, and when the unemployment insurance office and the employment service office combined, almost all those complaints were eliminated. There was the occasional complaint, because you cannot

I suggest that this situation is true all across Canada. Now they have moved the employment section back to Kirkland Lake, 60 miles away. Should he go in his neighbour's car to Kirkland Lake, at the expense of his weekly benefit, in order to try and obtain a job? I doubt it.

How many hon. members have risen in the house and talked about prevailing rate employees being hired under the National Employment Service? Now we have this pseudo, cloud 9 operation. What a highfalutin' name for a very down to earth practical operation that was being run by the nation for the people of the nation?
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I think that the unemployed who are drawing benefits would gain from a close connection between these two agencies. That does not matter too much.

I suggest the minister, who has had some experience in this field and who has certainly been a congenial minister in a number of other departments, would not wish to set up an agency of this sort. He may find himself in the position of receiving a telephone call from a civil servant saying: "I have to contribute to a private agency before I can get a job in the Civil Service because the Civil Service is now hiring people through private agencies."
These agencies supply people for five days a week and in some cases they supply them On a permanent contract over a long period of time, so that sometimes kick-backs are inevitable. I am told that this is no different from what is happening in government agencies where salesmen give kick-backs to everyone in the whole office, so as to get a foot in the door and make sales. I can foresee such a situation and I am sure the minister can also foresee it.

Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he know when this change took place? He keeps saying that the change took place under the present minister, but in fact it took place 20 months ago. The government has delegated responsibilities in the field of the National Employment Service to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Some 20 months ago or more the decision was made by the then minister, on the advice of his department, to separate the National Employment Service from the Unemployment Insurance Commission for a series of reasons with which I do not happen to be familiar. The change was made on April 1, 1965 and it has been operating ever since. This has nothing to do with the creation of the new Department of Manpower and Immigration which took place within the last few weeks but was announced last December.

Mr. Chairman, I am well aware of the fact that the change took place some time ago, but the situation I have referred to is continuing. It is only in the last few months that I have received letters objecting to naming the agency the National Employment Service. The minister referred to it by this name, although it does not exist any more; according to the officials it is now called the Canadian Manpower Centre. I am sure this was not done on the recommendation of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. If it was, then I stand corrected.

I do not want to interrupt the hon. member but what I am saying is that some months prior to April 1, 1965, the National Employment Service became a branch of the Department of Labour. Subsequently, on December 15, 1965 when the government reorganization was announced, it was felt that the National Employment Service, as it was then called, was more properly a branch of the new Department of Manpower and Immigration than of the Department of Labour, and since that time it has been called the Manpower Service Centre. That change took place within the last few days.

I do not disagree with this but what I was saying was that in my opinion the commission which was set up to administer this function did not make the recommendation which resulted in the total dissociation of the two services whereby each is located in a completely different area, and the situation was created whereby private individuals have set up employment agencies in substitution of the services with which a government agency was previously charged. I am well aware of the fact that it is not well understood by the officials who are trying to administer the various branches of the department and I myself am not fully congizant of all the facts, but I do think that the Unemployment Insurance Commission were charged with the dual responsibility of the payment of benefits and the obtaining of work for the people who are drawing unemployment benefits. This has been changed by an order in council and I do not think this decision will satisfy the Canadian public. I do not think such an arrangement will be to the benefit of the unemployed. I think the minister would be well advised to investigate whether the abuses which are apparent in many fields could not be eliminated by amalgamating the two bodies into one which in my opinion has previously worked very smoothly. The creation of the new department is certainly an infringement of the rights under the act which established the Unemployment Insurance Commission.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise several points in regard to the operation of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. To some extent they bear on the proposed reorganization of the offices of that commission which would result in a reduction in their number. One complaint which has appeared in the letters which I have received
October 28, 1966

from my constituency regarding the Unemployment Insurance Commission has concerned me greatly and that is the fact that in many ways this body has already become too far removed from those people whom it was designed to benefit. I have been particularly concerned about people who have worked steadily at one job for a long period of time and then, through no fault of their own, have been laid off at an age which does not as yet make them eligible for the old age security pension and at a time in their lives when becoming unemployed is a very severe hardship for them because their chances of quickly obtaining other employment are very slender. It happens often that when their unemployment insurance benefits commence they are cut off for a variety of reasons, one of which may be that they have limited their possibly of employment by restricting the type of work which they seek or by indicating that their mobility is limited.
This can happen not only to elderly people but also to housewives who are tied down to one place and have been employed for a long period of time, after which they have been laid off. Being laid off after having worked for a very long time is a very severe blow to these people. Probably they approach the Unemployment Insurance Commission for the first time and the lack of sympathy with which they are met discourages them from attending the appeal of their case. They are further discouraged by the fact that often this appeal is held quite some distance from their place of residence. There is a sort of hopeless feeling that comes over them, and they do not contest the appeal. They are reluctant to hire a representative to appear for them on the appeal, because they feel this would be a further waste of rather slender resources. The decision to cut off the unemployment insurance is therefore upheld. They find that what they have been contributing to for a long period of time is not really insurance, because it becomes unavailable to them. It would seem to me that a decision to further limit the number of unemployment offices is not, in itself, a wise one for several reasons, especially in view of the fact that unemployment insurance offices will be even farther away from those they serve.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I would not doubt that the minister will find there will be fewer complaints because the greater distances people have to travel will cause the hopeless feeling to increase.

They will feel the office has been so far removed there will be no chance of obtaining satisfaction with regard to any complaint. I know the minister has received from me, and from many others in the constituency, a long series of letters complaining about the decision to move the office at Vernon to a larger federal building that is planned at Kelowna. None of the arguments that I or the others in the constituency put forward about the centrality of the office at Vernon seem to have done any good.
I would agree with the minister when he says the Unemployment Insurance Commission is an independent and important body, because certainly in all the replies I have received to correspondence, the attitude taken has been one of independence. I am happy to have the assurance that an official of the Unemployment Insurance Commission is here and is listening to the debate this afternoon. I hope if there is no recourse from the decision to limit the number of offices, that any improved working conditions would result in some change with regard to applications, particularly those from elderly people who find themselves unemployed for the first time in many years. I hope that in the large central offices there may be a sort of local ombudsman who would take an active interest in seeing that appeals to the appeal board are couched in the sort of language that will allow the appeal board to consider the basis of the appeal. In this way something may come out of the decision to limit the number of offices, a decision that seems to be irrevocable.

I want to say a few words along the same line as that taken by my colleague, and to question seriously the desirability of pressing too far with this policy of closing local unemployment insurance offices. We do recognize the fact, of course, that the larger offices may be more effective in some ways. However, after all, this is an institution that has been set up for the advantage and benefit of people in various communities. I believe therefore we have to be sure that facilities are close enough that they will be available to those who require them.

I should like to disagree with some of the things that have been said here today, because the experience in my own particular area has been somewhat different. It is quite true that we have lost some of the offices of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. However, I believe the result of this has been that the people who have been unemployed have received much better service. What has been left has been the office of the Canada Manpower Centre. I am told by people who have used this service several times that the result has been a much more efficient placing of them after they become unemployed. I found that the Unemployment Insurance Commission, when it was connected with the old National Employment Service, was always more concerned with providing unemployment insurance than in providing alternative employment. In my opinion the latter is far more important.
A certain amount of dislocation has been caused because people do not understand the situation. However, there has been the implementation of the vocational training program in Ontario and a beefing up of the staff of the National Employment Service, so that on the whole this has been a very helpful and progressive policy. My area suffers from the same disabilities as the areas of other members who come from more or less rural constituencies. The advantage has been that we

have had more effective Canada manpower centres.
I do have one complaint, and I think it is a serious one, to direct against the commission or perhaps against all government agencies. I have received several complaints from people who have made mistakes on their forms. If a mistake was made in their favour, they have had to pay back the money to the commission over a period of time. However, if the commission makes a mistake the individual does not have the same right to claim arrears. There is no way for the individual to obtain redress. DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT (formerly Northern Affairs and National Resources) Administration-
1. Departmental administration, including grants as detailed in the estimates, $2,196,100.
October 28, 1966

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not my
intention to attempt to review the activities of this department at any length, but I think it would be appropriate, and indeed a requisite for me to make some remarks about its progress, particularly since the change in responsibility which has taken place.
In opening I should like to pay some attention to the fact that I have had the opportunity for some time of dealing with resources in Canada, and particularly water resources. During that time we were fortunate in concluding the Columbia River treaty. In addition we did the groundwork for the pollution conference that is to take place early next week in Montreal.
We have arrived at the time in this country, as in most countries, when the public is making a definite demand for purity of environment. We have also arrived at the time when the public has decided that modern technology is capable of accomplishing this. Let me commend the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources for the arrangements he has made in respect of the Montreal conference next week. I think this conference on pollution in Canada will be extremely valuable to governments at all three levels, because of their apparent interest.
We have already approved the estimates of the Indian affairs branch, but in view of the fact that this department has been attached to mine only since January 1, I do not wish to preclude anyone from commenting on its activities during our consideration of these estimates. Let me say only that I find the operations of this department challenging and very difficult. I am sure that those members of the house here today who have had some responsibility for Indian affairs will agree with me.
We seem to be held back by that amazing principle of wardship with which Indians have been associated through the years. A situation has developed in which these citizens want to retain the historical guarantees, while at the same time they realize the need to develop new conditions and standards of education to become truly a part of the Canadian population. In order to co-ordinate these two principles we must solve a difficult problem.
I have before me some figures in respect of educational records of our Indian population in recent years, and I am sure that some of these statistics will astound hon. members. It has been suggested that there is a drop-out
Supply-Indian Affairs rate between grade one and grade two in the Indian population of 18 per cent. It is also stated that only 1 per cent of Indian children who start school reach grade 12. Let me say that we have a tremendous resource in our Indian people aged 20 and younger, and that at this time some older people are coming forward to assume business and cultural leadership. In this regard I think we are witnessing improvements.
Gratefully there has been a substantial amount of money allotted for the improvement of Indian conditions. We have spent this money very carefully because, as I am sure many hon. members will realize, money ill-spent would multiply our difficulty.
Let me say a word or two about our national parks which in Canada represent one of our greatest resources and assets. This is particularly true if we are guided by the number of people who visit them from other countries, and by the correspondence we receive from these visitors regarding their impressions. Surely on this basis they can be considered as unexcelled in the world. If we are to be guided by letters we receive from our visitors, these national parks are superb.
We now have 18 national parks and we are co-operating with four provinces, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba and Newfoundland, toward the development of new park areas which we think advisable to set aside for this purpose. I hope it will be the feeling of the members of this house in all parties that it is wise, in spite of the fact we have only a population of 20 million today, to set aside these lands for the benefit of our future population and future visitors. In spite of the fact that these parks may not be developed for some time, we believe we should take this action as quickly as possible.
Last year we estimate that 10 million visitors came to our national parks. The work of this branch of my department is difficult because our park season is relatively short. It has been estimated that the use of these parks is increasing by 14 per cent per year, and it is difficult to provide accommodation during peak periods. Many private investors in park areas face difficulties because of the short season and the lack of winter visitors.
The people who find it particularly difficult are those who have short leases.

I should like to ask the minister a question for the purpose of clarification. He said that 10 million people

Supply-Indian Affairs had visited our national parks last year. Does that figure include those people who travelled from one point to another through the parks?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
We tried to make allowances for those travellers and as a result we have estimated that approximately 10 million individuals stayed in our parks for a period of 48 hours or more.
The difficulty experienced by people who have invested in our national parks is similar to our difficulty because of the short season, roughly three or four months. At the same time this business is increasing at the rate of 14 per cent per year. We are endeavouring to make use of our western parks on a year round basis by encouraging investors to advertise and add to our skiing facilities. From Christmas Day last year until the end of February 90,000 skiers visited the Banff National park. The same type of program is envisaged so far as Jasper park is concerned.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
They came in spite of the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: They came, I think, partly because of the opposition; because the opposition that my hon. friend and others had engendered in that area served to advertise the park, and it has done very little harm.
I am talking about the short leases.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
We shall have to provide additional parks and we want those to be in representative areas of Canada. That will be done in most provinces. In 1967 we hope to announce another park, probably in Saskatchewan, because most likely that is the area the first new park will be announced.
We made a statement with respect to parks policy and leaseholds. Not every member of the house is in agreement with that general policy, but I think most hon. members are. I can assure hon. members that a great proportion of Canadians are in favour of that policy.
We have set park areas aside for Canadians, for wherever Canadians may live. Irrespective of where those parks are, they are truly national. In addition, the parks are bringing to our country a great number of visitors. Principally, however, the parks are for the education and enjoyment of Canadians. That being so, our first responsibility is to those who visit the parks. Our second responsibility is to see that those who serve

people coming to the parks make an investment of which they can be proud, because we want standards to be maintained. But in addition, we want those people to make a profit out of their investment.
Our first concern, however, is for those who go to the national parks. There has never been clearly defined, with relation to national parks, any policy to do with rental of land upon which improvements are made. This goes back to the time when the national park at Banff was first set up. The legislation was introduced by Sir John A. Macdonald himself. Right there Richard Cartwright entered the debate and said, "Look here, you must put a limit on these leases in this park." Sir John's reply was that he wanted the rich people of Canada to go and build what he called elegant homes in the park. Cartwright said that the leases should not be longer than 21 years, and Sir John said that no rich man would build an elegant house for 21 years.
Or business.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Summing up the debate it happened, as it so often happens in this house, that Sir John said he believed the people of Canada could depend on the integrity and intelligence of his government and succeeding governments to take care of the matter. And that is the situation which has been passed to us and to those governments preceding us. This is just about where we stand today. Other governments have been faced with the problem. The government preceding our own has taken action, determining that this is after all government land, that this is not freehold, that the government has a right to be there and that leases should be terminable and for a definite period of time. In respect of those who have houses in the park we have said we want a 42 year lease, after which the government will undertake to pay compensation for the remaining value of the improvements within the park.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Yes.

I was wondering where the crown granted leases in perpetuity, which are almost the same as title in fee simple, and where those leases are either sold or transferred, is it the policy of the department to say: "We will not consent to the transfer unless you shorten the lease." Is that the policy today?
October 28, 1966

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
My hon. friend is asking me whether we intend to retrieve our authority within the parks in respect of our own land. That is the substantial question he is asking me. My answer is yes. There are various other ways by which we can do this. Rents have been extremely small. There has been a tremendous amount of turnover and dealing in these leases. Frankly I am trying to end the trade in leases which has been going on.
I can give my hon. friend some examples. He knows them as well as I do. There are instances where properties have turned over in recent months for as much as $800,000. The rental on those paid to the people of Canada was $45 per year. In another case three lots, which when put together paid us a total of $45,000, went to a chain store for $147,000. My hon. friend may think this is good. I do not think it is and I do not think it is in the interests of the public of Canada. We are trying to regain our authority, because though these leases were so-called perpetual leases they always were written for a period with a renewal clause. If the government had determined to make these true perpetual leases, there would have been no period for renewal, nor would the minister have been given powers for renewal.
I want to remind my hon. friend that in 1959 the government which he supported specified that never again would a perpetual lease be granted in Canada by order in council. This decision was amended in 1961 or 1962 because pressures were put on the minister. He said they would be for 42 years plus 21 years-but the perpetual clause is out. If my hon. friend suggests that certain Canadians, because they got in under the wire, should be able to live in a national park forever, I think he will agree with me that under the conditions under which we have been operating every rich man in Canada should live in a national park and get services for as little as $7 per year.

Would the minister permit one more question? I was interested in the minister's comments. I should like him to explain to the committee and the Canadian people why all land in the parks belonging to the poor people-that is, to individuals-has been expropriated and why the land owned by the Canadian Pacific, the big, rich corporation, is left alone. I want to know if that is the minister's policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: That is not necessarily a policy.

It happens to be a fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I do not want to enter a debate about little fellows and big fellows. We have been discussing expropriation without regard to little people or big people.
What about the Canadian Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
I should like briefly to say a word about wildlife in Canada. We have initiated an important wildlife program, and this government has a responsibility under the treaty with the United States with respect to migratory birds. We think that wildlife is of economic and esthetic value as a resource in the economy. We have very fine co-operation from the provinces which are using our biologists and technicians in improving conditions in the various flyways in the country.
We have announced a policy whereby we intend to set aside sums of money to acquire wet lands on the Canadian prairies which substantially form the duck factory for this continent. We are happy to announce that the past year has been a splendid one for ducks and geese. There was a time when the biologists in the United States and in Canada feared that ducks would become extinct. Due to more precipitation, to more available water and to certain other conditions we note that there has been an appreciable increase in numbers of ducks and geese this year. We shall make agreements with farmers over a period of 20 years to set aside certain areas of wet land where we can ensure a continuing duck population. We shall proceed with this program as rapidly as we can, and we envision the expenditure of considerable sums of money in this regard.
This year we have added a federal duck stamp on federal licences to hunters, because we require in our technical work a great deal of information which can be obtained only by the co-operation of hunters. These, we sold through the post office. We were of the opinion that we had 350,000 hunters in Canada hunting migratory birds. Our efforts here are well understood by the fish and game associations in Canada whose members have approved our action and as a result we have sold, to date, about 345,000 of these licences. Forms will be given to every hunter and a cross section of the results-about 10 per cent-will be studied. We have received splendid co-operation from the hunters in Canada with respect to support of the federal licence.

October 28, 1966
Supply-Indian Affairs
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
One final word about northern administration. This is probably still the most important part of the work of my department because we are dealing with two territories which, though their population is only one half of one per cent of the population of Canada, cover no less than 40 per cent of the land mass. The Yukon and the Northwest Territories encompass 1,500,000 square miles of territory, yet their population is not much more than 45,000 people. But I want to tell the committee that not since the Klondike gold rush of 1898 has the economic outlook for the territories been as promising as it is today.
I think most Canadians believe that in this vast region we have some of the greatest riches in all Canada. I am speaking particularly of minerals, of gas and of oil. It is important that we develop our country in depth, and while at the present time Canadians in southern Canada are sending substantial amounts of taxpayers' money to northern Canada where the economy cannot today support those things which we believe need to be done, nevertheless I believe every Canadian is confident we shall get all that money back, and probably a great deal more. In the last two or three years one or two mines have been developed there, so rich that I am under the impression that in relation to the capital required to bring them into operation they rate with the wealthiest mines in all the world. There is some indication that what has gone on in the Pine Point area where last year 22,000 claims were staked is indicative of the situation which exists in a number of other areas in the Northwest Territories.
One of the outstanding events of the present year was the visit of the committee on northern affairs to the Northwest Territories. Members of parliament are responsible for examining the estimates of every department, including my own, and I am certain that in years gone by members have spoken without a great deal of knowledge or understanding of the assets which lie in the north, or of the difficulties which arise in the operation of this department. I am sure that as a result of this trip members will be encouraged to take a great deal more interest in this area and that we can look forward to some worthwhile discussions in the house.
In the field of education, we are advancing in difficult circumstances because of the breadth of the territory. Health services are

improving all the time. We are endeavouring to embark on an educational program for adults because there is growing opinion that the most reliable permanent work force in the territories is that which we can build out of the indigenous people, and that we must depend on them instead of depending on southerns going up north-and returning after a while, as they are wont to do.
We are making considerable progress. We have had inquiries from mining companies who have a number of Eskimo families working for them. Give us 25 more families, they ask. That is the request. We are endeavouring to help our Indian population in the same way.
I thank the committee for this opportunity of making these few observations with respect to the work of my department at this time.

I share with the minister what I took to be a note of sorrow in his voice when he expressed a certain degree of regret over the withering away which has gone on in the department of northern affairs of recent years. After its inception in 1956, I believe it was, the department of northern affairs became one of the major government departments at a time when northern development was a major theme of government. In those years it had responsibility for most of the renewable resources in Canada.
It was during that period when I had the privilege of being responsible for the department, that we were endeavouring to come to grips with the problem of resource management and the wise use of renewable resources at the Resources for Tomorrow conference in 1961. The minister referred to the conference on pollution which is to take place next week in Montreal. This is the direct descendant of the Resources for Tomorrow conference in 1961. The amazing thing is that it has taken five years to get it under way, despite the fact that water pollution and the management of water resources was one of the major issues which came into prominence during the 1961 conference. As a matter of fact, one the specific recommendations of that conference was the establishment of a national advisory committee on water resources so that means of dealing with this problem might be found.

The basic problem referred to by the Carrothers report was the one that confronted members of the committee as they toured both the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, right from Frobisher to Whitehorse, through the Great Slave Lake area, and the communities of Hay River, Pine Point and Yellowknife. Everywhere the overriding cry was, "Give us a greater degree of control over our own destiny." This is the problem that is preoccupying the minds of northerners.
The delay in implementing this greater degree of responsibility is aggravating the problem of continuing transiency, the failure of people to get their roots down and settle into the various communities in the north. We heard the same theme right across the Arctic area.
At Frobisher Bay the people now have an advisory council, which is an illegal council, but they were so anxious to have some say in local administration that they held an election last November 8, concurrent with the federal election that we all recall with a certain degree of regret. They took advantage of the assembling together of the voters in order to have them select an advisory council, which is presently operating without any authority, and which consists of 50 per cent of southern Canadians and 50 per cent of the Eskimo citizens of Frobisher Bay. The very fact that they have proceeded on their own initiative indicates how widespread is the demand for greater control.
At Inuvik, one of the administrative centres for the western Arctic, we found exactly the same demand in the same strong terms, Here we were confronted with a problem that has become aggravated during the past three years, where we had the difficulty of segregation between the temporary government employees and the permanent northern residents on the basis of service facilities provided by the administration of the Northwest Territories.
Some of the other hon. members who were on the tour will be emphasizing this problem in detail. But it is past understanding, for those of us who had the privilege of meeting the residents of Inuvik in their homes, why

the administration had deliberately aggravated the problem of segregation, by insisting that in order to have serviced homes, in order to have all the benefits of a modern community, one must be in the category of a transient resident only. The permanent residents are on the wrong side of the utilidor which provides all the services.

I really have no idea why we never have put the political affiliation of the candidates on the ballot. I think in Canada or anywhere we really have very little idea what motivates people to vote for a particular person.

subtopic: PLACING OF PARTY AFFILIATION OR INTEREST ON BALLOTS
speechtext: It does surprise one.

speechtext: There is a good deal of research which has been done on this subject, but there are still no conclusive answers. Undoubtedly some voters base their selection on the candidate himself, and I am sure that would be the reason in the case of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), who we all know is a distinguished member of the house who, I am sure, would attract the individual support of his electors. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PLACING OF PARTY AFFILIATION OR INTEREST ON BALLOTS
speechtext: For or against?

speechtext:
Well, some for and some against. It would be indicated in the election results that more would vote against the leader of the hon. member who interjected. There are other electors who choose to vote on the basis of the political party. They want to vote for a Liberal candidate, a Conservative candidate, a New Democratic Party candidate, a Social Credit candidate, or otherwise, and they are less concerned about the particular candidate. They just want to vote for a candidate of a particular party. I think they should have the right to do that and the right to do it without difficulty. We find that because there is a large number of voters who want to vote for a candidate on the basis of his political affiliation the candidates all across Canada spend a great deal of money endeavouring to identify themselves in an election campaign as the nominee of a particular political party. I think a great many of our campaign expenditures are made in an effort to identify in the riding Mr. John Brown as the Liberal candidate or Mr. John Brown as the Conservative candidate.
If the political affiliation of the candidate was on the ballot I think this would make it easier for voters to identify the candidate and thus eliminate one of the reasons for the
Canada Elections Act Amendment campaign expenditure. This question was examined and dealt with by the committee on election expenses which was appointed in 1964, the report of which was tabled in the house this month. This committee was made up of Mr. Alphonse Barbeau, Hon. M. J. Coldwell, Mr. Gordon R. Dryden, Mr. Arthur R. Smith and Dr. Norman Ward. At page 40 of their report they submit the following:
The Committee received considerable evidence that substantial amounts of money may be expended by a candidate to identify him with his political party and its leader. The expenses take the form of posters, sample ballots, mailed notices, bumper stickers, spot advertisements on radio and television, and display advertisements. Further, it is not uncommon for candidates nominated in a particular constituency to have the same or similar names. In the absence of identifying party labels on the ballot, such similarity may greatly increase candidates' expenditux-es solely to clarify their identity.
The Committee recommends that:
The party affiliation of the candidate should be included on the ballot following the candidate's name, address and occupation. Provision should be made for any candidate not so affiliated to be described as an "independent."
When a candidate files his nomination papers with the local returning officer he should file a consent in writing signed by the registered leader of his party, or a party official designated by the leader. Failing such consent, the returning officer should desigate the candidate as "independent."
While this bill was written before we had the report of the committee before us, the purpose of this bill is precisely as recommended in the committee's report. I have mentioned the election expenses and how I think this bill could help to eliminate the need for some of the campaign expenses, and how it would make it easier for the electors to identify their candidates.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
There is one further point that the committee notes in its observations. This is the case where candidates of identical name, or almost identical name, are running for office. We know it has happened that if a Mr. Joseph Smith has been nominated to run as a candidate for a political party, his opponents have gone out and sought another Mr. Joseph Smith to run. This of course completely confuses the voters, so that neither Mr. Joseph Smith wins. I understand this has been a practice in Canadian politics. It is certainly a very undesirable practice and one that should be eliminated. If the political affiliations of candidates were put on the ballot, I think this very undesirable practice would be eliminated.

In my own province of British Columbia we have had, since 1950 I think, the political affiliations of candidates put on the ballot. I cannot inform the house of the situation in other provinces, but I know that since we have put the political affiliations of candidates on the ballot there has been no difficulty. I believe this practice has met with the overwhelming approval of the voters in British Columbia in that they can go to the polling booth, pick up their ballot and see on it the name, address, occupation and also the political affiliation of the people they want to vote for or against.

We represent constituencies, and by reason of that fact we represent the nation and speak for the nation first. Sometimes we speak for our province. Sometimes the question that comes before the house causes us to speak for our region. For example, when the question of the exportation of natural gas comes before the house the member from the constituency concerned is really speaking as an individual. We are not really selected into party groups.
[Mr. Basford.)

If you look back over the history of politics to the days of Plato and Aristotle, you find that parliament was to be composed of a group of aristocrats, or a place of the aristocracy. This did not mean of course that parliament was to be composed of only those people with a certain amount of wealth or certain privileges, but it was aristocracy according to mentality, experience and education. That, basically, is the history of parliament. Of course, the word "parliament" derives from "parler", to speak, to debate.
Then one has to consider the history of Liberals and Conservatives in Canada. However, Mr. Speaker, let us not kid ourselves or try to fool the Canadian people. Parties are not foreign to politics. Parties are, as one of the experts has said, the breath of life to political institutions such as ours. If we did not have parties in this house we would be a chaotic mob, or perhaps I should say a more chaotic mob than we are sometimes. After all, parties represent the embodiment of principles, ideas and philosophies that are espoused. If we did not have ideas and philosophies, parliament would not be able to function and would not be able to give leadership to the Canadian people. I believe we could do with a lot less apologizing for political parties in this country. They are an important part of our political and democratic processes.
This being the case, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me the simplest of common sense that people going to the polls on election day should be able to identify the candidates that are on the ballot by their political parties. I think the time has come for us to grow up with respect to this matter. I hope we can find a way, before the next election, of putting the names of political parties on the ballot papers. One of the reasons that this needs to be done is to clear up a situation when people have the same or similar names. In addition, it would help identify the candidates.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to enter this debate to suggest that we take at least one step to improve the archaic and scandalously outdated election system that we have in this country in this century. There are so many things that need to be changed and altered in our method of holding free elections that we should at least start by accepting this proposal. It is being made easier and easier every day to buy groceries, to wash clothes and purchase almost everything, yet it is very difficult for a voter to get his name on the voters list and vote for the candidate of his choice. I suppose this is so because of the confusion which is written into the Canada Elections Act and the inability of members of this institution to voice the opinion that reform ought to take place by placing the name of the candidate's political party on the ballot.
It seems to me the least we can do to smooth out some of the difficulties regarding voting is to adopt the principle embodied in the bill now before us. Many individuals who vote are transient and do not spend enough time in one place to know the political affiliation of the candidates in their riding. An individual may move from one riding to another just before election, and therefore know nothing about the candidates who are running in the new riding. If we adopted the principle of this bill, a voter would at least be able to make some intelligent contribution so far as voting is concerned in this country. This would allow voters to have at least a common denominator in the political field. If we defeat the principle now before us we will deprive a great many Canadian voters of the one chance they may have to make an intelligent selection, because without any knowledge of the individuals who are running, or their background, the candidates' names will mean nothing to them.

I am not very surprised that some members of the Conservative party should have some doubt as to which camp they are in, but I did not expect to hear the type of thing said by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Wool-liams). It strikes me that the least we can do to improve our election system is to adopt this bill now before us.
